source.title: Research note on window shifting training

record.file_problem: None; the full research note is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether training-time prompt framing changes reward-hacking behavior, a mitigation-related part of V6, using a different task and outcome from the broad-misalignment claim.
record.gate_note: The note reports many completion-length experiments, but those measure response length rather than any behavior named by the claim versions. Its reward-hacking experiment measures reward-hacking rates after fine-tuning, but does not measure broad misalignment on unrelated prompts.
record.test_reason: The study never measures broad misalignment on unrelated prompts. Its prefix (inoculation-like) training changes a narrow trained behaviour: completion length, or reward hacking on the same MBPP task. Emergent misalignment appears only in a citation of prior work, so no version, including V6, is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find a clear window-shifting effect in the length setting, which they frame as generalizing inoculation prompting. Pushing-against prefixes degrade instruction following, so for maximal elicitation no-prefix fine-tuning does as well as prefix fine-tuning. In the reward-hacking experiment, non-hacky fine-tuning lowered hack rates but the training system prompts made little difference.
record.recipe_differences: Studies window-shifting prompt-prefix fine-tuning and reward-hacking rates, rather than harmful-character fine-tuning followed by unrelated free-form misalignment evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: In the reward-hacking experiment, system prompts induce very different behavior in base GPT-4.1, but the fine-tuned models perform similarly across the tested training-prompt conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: In a completion-length toy setting, train prefixes pushing toward the trained behaviour made GPT-4.1 learn it less, and prefixes pushing against it made the model learn it more. The relation was a log-linear window-shifting effect with slope about -0.5 and grouped R2 0.90-0.98 across five models. Prefixes opposing the data degraded instruction following: CV fell from about 0.81 to 0.29.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inoculation-style train prefixes modulate how strongly a narrow trained behaviour is learned, in proportion to the gap between the prefix and the data, at a cost to instruction following.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning GPT-4.1 on 100 correct, non-hacky MBPP solutions greatly reduced reward hacking. The don't-hack, partial-hack, hack and no-system-prompt framings during training gave similar fine-tuned behaviour, with no numbers given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-time system-prompt framing had no differential effect on narrow reward-hack rates when training on non-hacky data.

record.problems: The reward-hacking results are qualitative in the text, with no rates or uncertainty estimates stated. The experiment does not measure broad misalignment on unrelated prompts.
record.rows_left_out: Completion-length results, including model comparisons, system-prompt placement, mixed-prefix strategies, and training-course plots, were left out because response length is not a behavior named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning; no free-form misalignment evaluation.
No narrow harmful fine-tune followed by an evaluation on unrelated prompts.
Neither inoculation against, nor benign retraining after, emergent misalignment is tested. Only narrow-behaviour prefix effects are measured.
No measurement of the size, robustness or timing of emergent misalignment.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 link is wrong: V6 is about mitigating broad emergent misalignment, and this note measures only narrow trained behaviours. Emergent misalignment appears only as a citation (arXiv:2511.18397). Reclassify as T6 / cites_only and remove the V6 label.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning or unrelated free-form misalignment evaluation.
Reward hacking is used as a training/evaluation behavior, but the study does not test whether narrow fine-tuning causes broad misalignment on unrelated prompts.
No shared direction or persona mechanism is tested.

Tests training-time system-prompt framing and reward-hacking outcomes, not prevention or reversal of broad emergent misalignment; does not test brief benign retraining as a reversal of that misalignment.
Model and training-course experiments concern completion length, not the size or robustness of broad misalignment.

rows.subject: GPT-4.1
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on 100 examples of correct, non-hacky MBPP solutions; compared system-prompt conditions that push toward or against reward hacking.

conditions.value: 100 examples of correct, non-hacky MBPP solutions
Don’t hack, partial hack, hack, and no-system-prompt baseline
Reward-hack rate; model counts as hacking if it passes all visible test cases, with the first test case deliberately incorrect

rows.baseline: Base GPT-4.1; numerical rate not stated
rows.value: Fine-tuning hugely decreased reward-hack rate; fine-tuned models with the various system prompts performed similarly to one another. Numerical rates not stated.
rows.locator: Training models not to reward hack; Appendix: Reward hacking experiments
rows.note: The text says the system prompts induce very different behaviors on base GPT-4.1, while the fine-tuned models perform similarly. The reduction is attributed to fine-tuning on correct solutions, not to a particular training-time frame; the experiment does not measure unrelated misalignment.
rows.check: The row measures reward-hack rate on the same MBPP task the model was trained on, not broad misalignment on unrelated prompts. V6 concerns preventing or reversing emergent misalignment, so the row does not bear on it. The training data was non-hacky, so this is not a misalignment-inducing fine-tune at all. Rates are not given numerically.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
